stories.brief: The history of public television in Israel: educational broadcasts began in 1966, followed by programming for the general public in 1968, after debate over television’s role in Israeli society.

sources.title: Israeli Educational Television
Educational Television Starts Broadcasting in Israel
“The Making of Israeli Television”—Debates Ahead of the Establishment of Israel TV 1948–1968
Israel Tests Television Transmission of Education Programs for Schools

storyBeats: Israel’s first television transmissions were educational broadcasts for schools, not programs for the general public.
Educational television began broadcasting in 1966; the National Library of Israel dates the first transmission to March 15.
The Rothschild Foundation financed the educational television system, which was intended to serve Israeli schools.
Early televised lessons included subjects such as mathematics, biology, and English.
The idea of television in Israel was debated for years before general public broadcasting began; the disagreement included questions about its likely cultural and social effects.
The scholarly account describes supporters as seeing television’s educational and social value, while others feared its cultural influence.
On May 2, 1968, Israel Television began with a pilot broadcast of a military parade.
The parade broadcast took place on Israel’s Independence Day, nearly a year after the Six-Day War.
The new general service and educational television represented two different uses of the screen: public broadcasting and lessons for pupils.

stories.brief: Leah Goldberg’s Hebrew children’s story “Room for Rent,” first published in 1948, uses a shared apartment building of animal characters to explore living together across differences.

sources.title: Leah Goldberg: Books and Stories
Two Pioneering Models before the Young Camp: Renovations in the Five-Story Building—Three Period Readings of Leah Goldberg’s “Room for Rent”
The story’s publication history and early editions
Educational material on “Room for Rent”

storyBeats: Leah Goldberg’s Hebrew story “Room for Rent” first appeared in the children’s newspaper Mishmar LaYeladim in October 1948.
The story is set in a five-story apartment tower in a beautiful valley among vineyards and fields.
The building’s animal residents include a hen, a cuckoo, a cat, and a squirrel; a vacant apartment on the top floor prompts the search for a new neighbor.
Prospective renters visit the apartment and judge the existing neighbors, giving the repeated apartment visits the story’s central pattern.
Several visitors reject the building because of a particular neighbor, rather than because the apartment itself is unsuitable.
The poem-like tale gives the animals human speech and turns an apartment search into a story about neighbors living together.
In the ending, the dove accepts the apartment and the neighbors; the scholarly reading notes that the building’s residents then form an all-female household of animals.
The story was issued as a standalone children’s book in 1959, with illustrations by Shoshana Heyman.
A later 1970 edition was illustrated by Shmuel Katz; the familiar book edition therefore differs from the story’s earlier newspaper appearance and first illustrated book edition.
The National Library records translations of the story into several languages, including English, Arabic, and German.

stories.brief: A 1957 Israeli film follows Jewish immigrants settling in the new town of Kiryat Nazareth, later Nof Hagalil, as they move into apartments and build homes while the developing town initially lacks jobs and electricity.

sources.title: Suburb in the Nazareth Mountains | 1957

sources.publisher: Israel Defense Forces and Defense Establishment Archive
sources.title: Upper Nazareth: The City Established by the Ministry of Defense
The Establishment of Textile-Nazareth
The Story of Nof HaGalil

storyBeats: A 1957 Israeli film follows Jewish immigrants arriving by ship and then traveling by bus to the hills near Nazareth, where the film calls the new settlement Kiryat Nazareth.
The film shows the newcomers first arriving in Nazareth itself, then seeing apartment blocks on the hillside as their intended new home.
The film presents the immigrants settling into apartments and helping to build additional housing.
In the film’s account, the settlement initially has no local employment source and its housing is not connected to the electricity grid.
A Polish immigrant boy guides viewers through places in his new routine, including a school and clinic.
The boy also visits the market in old Nazareth, which the film says gradually grows on him.
The film ends by imagining the developing settlement as a future production and administrative center for the Galilee.
The settlement was part of a state development effort to establish a Jewish town alongside Nazareth and to settle immigrants there.
Because the new town needed jobs for its immigrant residents, the state sought to attract industry; one scholarly account describes substantial proposed government loans for a textile factory.
The Defense Ministry’s archive describes its unusually broad role in the settlement’s early municipal needs, including bringing in factories and supplying cloth for school uniforms.
The place’s name changed over time: it was called Kiryat Nazareth in the film, later Nazareth Illit, and is now Nof HaGalil.

stories.brief: The history of public television in Israel: educational broadcasts began in 1966, followed by programming for the general public in 1968, after debate over television’s role in Israeli society.

sources.title: Israeli Educational Television
Educational Television Starts Broadcasting in Israel
“The Making of Israeli Television”—Debates Ahead of the Establishment of Israel TV 1948–1968
Israel Tests Television Transmission of Education Programs for Schools

storyBeats: Israel’s first television transmissions were educational broadcasts for schools, not programs for the general public.
Educational television began broadcasting in 1966; the National Library of Israel dates the first transmission to March 15.
The Rothschild Foundation financed the educational television system, which was intended to serve Israeli schools.
Early televised lessons included subjects such as mathematics, biology, and English.
The idea of television in Israel was debated for years before general public broadcasting began; the disagreement included questions about its likely cultural and social effects.
The scholarly account describes supporters as seeing television’s educational and social value, while others feared its cultural influence.
On May 2, 1968, Israel Television began with a pilot broadcast of a military parade.
The parade broadcast took place on Israel’s Independence Day, nearly a year after the Six-Day War.
The new general service and educational television represented two different uses of the screen: public broadcasting and lessons for pupils.

stories.brief: Leah Goldberg’s Hebrew children’s story “Room for Rent,” first published in 1948, uses a shared apartment building of animal characters to explore living together across differences.

sources.title: Leah Goldberg: Books and Stories
Two Pioneering Models before the Young Camp: Renovations in the Five-Story Building—Three Period Readings of Leah Goldberg’s “Room for Rent”
The story’s publication history and early editions
Educational material on “Room for Rent”

storyBeats: Leah Goldberg’s Hebrew story “Room for Rent” first appeared in the children’s newspaper Mishmar LaYeladim in October 1948.
The story is set in a five-story apartment tower in a beautiful valley among vineyards and fields.
The building’s animal residents include a hen, a cuckoo, a cat, and a squirrel; a vacant apartment on the top floor prompts the search for a new neighbor.
Prospective renters visit the apartment and judge the existing neighbors, giving the repeated apartment visits the story’s central pattern.
Several visitors reject the building because of a particular neighbor, rather than because the apartment itself is unsuitable.
The poem-like tale gives the animals human speech and turns an apartment search into a story about neighbors living together.
In the ending, the dove accepts the apartment and the neighbors; the scholarly reading notes that the building’s residents then form an all-female household of animals.
The story was issued as a standalone children’s book in 1959, with illustrations by Shoshana Heyman.
A later 1970 edition was illustrated by Shmuel Katz; the familiar book edition therefore differs from the story’s earlier newspaper appearance and first illustrated book edition.
The National Library records translations of the story into several languages, including English, Arabic, and German.

stories.brief: A 1957 Israeli film follows Jewish immigrants settling in the new town of Kiryat Nazareth, later Nof Hagalil, as they move into apartments and build homes while the developing town initially lacks jobs and electricity.

sources.title: Suburb in the Nazareth Mountains | 1957

sources.publisher: Israel Defense Forces and Defense Establishment Archive
sources.title: Upper Nazareth: The City Established by the Ministry of Defense
The Establishment of Textile-Nazareth
The Story of Nof HaGalil

storyBeats: A 1957 Israeli film follows Jewish immigrants arriving by ship and then traveling by bus to the hills near Nazareth, where the film calls the new settlement Kiryat Nazareth.
The film shows the newcomers first arriving in Nazareth itself, then seeing apartment blocks on the hillside as their intended new home.
The film presents the immigrants settling into apartments and helping to build additional housing.
In the film’s account, the settlement initially has no local employment source and its housing is not connected to the electricity grid.
A Polish immigrant boy guides viewers through places in his new routine, including a school and clinic.
The boy also visits the market in old Nazareth, which the film says gradually grows on him.
The film ends by imagining the developing settlement as a future production and administrative center for the Galilee.
The settlement was part of a state development effort to establish a Jewish town alongside Nazareth and to settle immigrants there.
Because the new town needed jobs for its immigrant residents, the state sought to attract industry; one scholarly account describes substantial proposed government loans for a textile factory.
The Defense Ministry’s archive describes its unusually broad role in the settlement’s early municipal needs, including bringing in factories and supplying cloth for school uniforms.
The place’s name changed over time: it was called Kiryat Nazareth in the film, later Nazareth Illit, and is now Nof HaGalil.
